title: Rapid Development
summary: Get your knights and bishops out fast, castle early, and connect your rooks.

steps.text: In the opening, your first job is to develop: bring knights and bishops off the back rank toward the center. Every move should put a new piece into play.
White played 1.e4 (grabbing center and freeing the bishop and queen) and 2.Nf3 — developing with a threat on e5. Black to move: develop a knight and defend the pawn.
steps.task: Find Black's most natural developing move.

steps.text: Both sides have one piece out. White should keep developing — the f1 bishop wants an active square.
steps.task: Develop White's light-squared bishop to its best diagonal.

steps.text: Black developed the g8 knight with an attack on e4 — development with tempo is ideal. White is ready to bring the king to safety.
steps.task: Complete White's development plan by securing the king.

steps.text: Model development: all four minor pieces out for both sides, White castled, rooks ready to connect. Rule of thumb: knights before bishops, castle by move 10, don't move the same piece twice without reason.

title: Control the Center
summary: Pawns and pieces that control e4, d4, e5 and d5 control the whole board.

steps.text: The four central squares (e4, d4, e5, d5) are the highway of the board. Pieces in the center attack in every direction; pieces on the rim are dim.
1.e4 stakes a claim in the center and opens lines for the bishop and queen. Black should fight for the center immediately — ignoring it means a cramped game.
steps.task: Black's most direct way to contest the center with a pawn.

steps.text: The Queen's Gambit: White offers a pawn to drag Black's d5 pawn away from the center. Taking on c4 is playable but concedes the center — Black usually supports d5 instead.
steps.task: Support Black's d5 pawn with a pawn.

steps.text: In the Open Sicilian, White traded the d-pawn for Black's c-pawn and has a knight on d4 dominating central squares. Piece occupation of the center is as important as pawns.
steps.task: Black develops while challenging White's e4 strongpoint.

steps.text: Summary: occupy the center with pawns when you can, support them with pieces, and trade your flank pawns for the opponent's center pawns — not the other way around.

title: King Safety First
summary: Castle early, keep pawn cover in front of your king, and punish an uncastled king.

steps.text: Both kings are still in the middle. The center can open at any moment, and a king stuck on e1 or e8 becomes a target for rooks and queens on the e-file.
steps.task: White to move: get the king safe right now.

steps.text: This is why pawn cover matters: Black's king is stalemated behind its own pawns with no luft (escape square). White's rook can strike immediately.
steps.task: Deliver the back-rank mate.

steps.text: Same idea, but Black has luft: the pawn on h6 gives the king g7/h7 squares, so Ra8+ would only be a check. When you attack, always count the king's escape squares first.
Black grabbed pawns but the king is still on e8 with the e-file half-open. White's development lead is worth real material.
steps.task: White to move: find the most forcing way to use the lead in development (hint: hit f7).

steps.text: When the king's pawn cover is intact but pieces are far away, direct piece sacrifices on h7 (the Greek Gift) become possible. Here the bishop on b1 already eyes h7.
steps.task: White crashes through — take on h7 with mate.

title: Pins and Forks
summary: The two most common tactical weapons: pin pieces to more valuable targets, fork two targets at once.

steps.text: The Ruy Lopez begins with a pin: the b5 bishop attacks the c6 knight, which is pinned in spirit to the e5 pawn's defense. A pinned piece is a poor defender.
Here the c6 knight is ABSOLUTELY pinned to the king on e8 — it literally cannot move. Attack a pinned piece again and it cannot run away.
steps.task: Win the pinned knight with a pawn.

steps.text: A knight fork attacks two (or more) targets simultaneously. The most devastating forks involve a check, because the opponent must answer the check and lose the second piece.
steps.task: Fork Black's king and queen with the knight.

steps.text: Another royal fork pattern: the knight lands on f7, checking the king on h8 while eyeing the queen on d8.
steps.task: Give the fork with check.

steps.text: Pins against the king are absolute. Black's queen on f7 cannot leave the c4-g8 diagonal, so the bishop simply takes it, conceding only itself.
steps.task: Cash in the pinned queen.

title: Pawn Breaks
summary: Pawn levers open files and diagonals: learn when to push c/d/e/f pawns to challenge the enemy structure.

steps.text: In the Queen's Gambit Declined, Black's problem piece is the c8 bishop and the key freeing break is ...c5. Pawn breaks are how you challenge a static structure.
Black is solid but cramped. The thematic lever is ...c7-c5, striking at d4 and freeing the c8 bishop and the queen.
steps.task: Play Black's freeing pawn break.

steps.text: In the Ruy Lopez, Black's queenside expansion ...b5 gave space; now the central break ...d6-d5 (the Marshall idea) is the dream, while White prepares d3-d4.
steps.task: White to move: strike in the center with the d-pawn.

steps.text: In the Najdorf, ...e5 kicked the knight but left the d5 square weak. Pawn breaks create weaknesses too — every push leaves squares behind. White will plant a piece on d5.
The French Defense: Black's whole counterplay rests on the ...c5 break attacking d4. Without pawn breaks, a cramped position stays cramped forever.
steps.task: White supports the center with a flank pawn (the most solid option).

title: Prophylaxis
summary: Ask: what does my opponent WANT to play? Preventing their idea is often stronger than pursuing your own.

steps.text: Black's most annoying idea here is ...Bg4, pinning the f3 knight and weakening White's grip on d4. Before starting your own plans, ask what the opponent wants.
steps.task: Play the prophylactic pawn move that stops ...Bg4.

steps.text: White dreams of e3-e4, but Black's ...Bb7 and ...c5 will hit the center first. Prophylaxis: secure your own structure before expanding.
Black threatens ...b5 and ...Bb7 with queenside play, and the immediate ...e5 kick is in the air. Karpov would ask: how do I limit Black's counterplay before it starts?
steps.task: Find the quiet move that keeps Black's ...b5 expansion under control.

steps.text: Prophylaxis is also defensive: White's back rank is weak (Ra8# ideas if the rook leaves). Creating luft for your own king before launching an attack is prophylactic thinking.
steps.task: Give White's king an escape square.

steps.text: Karpov's signature: small moves like h3, a3, Kh1, Rg1 that take squares away from the opponent. When you are ahead in development, prophylaxis preserves it; when behind, it keeps you alive.

title: Piece Activity
summary: Rooks belong on open files, knights on outposts, bishops on long diagonals. Maximize every piece.

steps.text: From a Scotch Four Knights: open files and outposts decide the middlegame. The e-file is half-open and the d6 square is tender — activity beats material symmetry.

White just expanded with b4, and the e1 rook stares at e5, but the knight on f3 has no future yet. Knights crave outposts — protected advanced squares where pawns can't chase them. d5 is White's dream square.
steps.task: Start the knight's journey to the d5 outpost (via e2 or h4).

steps.text: The d5 square has no black pawn that can ever chase a piece away (the d-pawn is gone, the e-pawn advanced). A knight on d5 would be a permanent thorn.
steps.task: Plant the knight on the d5 outpost.

steps.text: An active rook on the 7th rank or an open file often equals a pawn. Here the e-file and the 7th rank beckon, and Black's queenside pawns are fixed targets.
steps.task: Invade with White's rook on the 7th rank.

steps.text: One more activity test: the knight on d4 has a beautiful outpost on c6/f5, but the most forcing active move wins material immediately.
steps.task: Find the knight fork that wins the exchange.

title: Essential Endgames
summary: King activity, the opposition, the square rule, and basic mating nets — the foundation of endgame skill.

steps.text: King and pawn vs king: White wins by using the king to escort the pawn. The key concept is the opposition — forcing the enemy king to give way.
steps.task: Push the pawn, gaining space with check.

steps.text: The square rule: if the enemy king can step inside the pawn's 'square' (count files = ranks to promotion), it catches the pawn. Otherwise the pawn runs free. Here White's own king blocks the pawn — in endgames, lead with the king.
steps.task: Centralize: bring the king in front of the pawn.

steps.text: Rook mates need the enemy king on the edge and your own king cutting off escape squares. White's king covers a7/b7/c7 — the rook only needs to give check along the 8th.
steps.task: Deliver mate in one.

steps.text: Promotion tactics: a pawn on the 7th with rook support is a monster. Here White can promote immediately — Black's rook will take, but White's rook recaptures with a winning material swing.
steps.task: Promote the pawn.

steps.text: Two rooks mate a bare king by 'ladder mate': one rook cuts off, the other checks, driving the king to the edge. Activate the rooks and finish.
steps.task: Give the mate in one with the back-rank rook.
